verdict: The Dutch instincts here are genuinely good – half twee, geen vs niet, de/het as the gatekeeper, pinnen and Tikkie at tier 1, hoor/even/maar as softeners, lekker and gezellig sprawling across senses – but the file is still a Hindi syllabus wearing Dutch clothes, and it shows in four structural ways. First, the scaffold leaks: roughly thirty-five learner-facing notes explain Dutch by reference to words this learner has never seen (baat hs-0057, khana hs-0063, roti hs-0156, dal hs-0158, ne hs-0249/0639, wālā hs-0253, jī hs-0245, bhābhī hs-0288, rickshaw hs-0315, sahab hs-0839, okra hs-0868, khilana hs-0894, UPI hs-1042, lakh hs-1063, plus "swapped in / fills the X slot / stands in for" at hs-0568, 0654, 0806, 0864, 1056, 1075, 1110, 1151). Second, the shape of the source deck survives the translation: twelve in-law terms, three items for gezin, three for fiets and about sixty food nouns, against nothing at all for vergadering, agenda, adres, betalen, huisarts, bon, thuiswerken, borrel, vakantie, zorgverzekering or DigiD – a Hindi home-life spine mapped onto a learner whose actual day is a commute, an office, a counter and a GP receptionist. Third, and most serious pedagogically, the grammar spine has holes a Dutch curriculum never has: there is no item for hij, no subject-pronoun set, no present tense of hebben, no V2 inversion rule (it hides in a note), no yes/no question formation, no stem-spelling rule so the tier-1 present tense cannot actually be produced, no niet placement, no te + infinitive, no diminutive formation, no reflexives, no particle system taught as a system, and no phonology whatsoever – while mogen, zien, vinden, verstaan, blijven, staan, want and wel exist only inside notes and chunks. Fourth, hygiene: I count around fifty duplicate pairs or triples, many with conflicting tiers (in tier 1 vs 3, op 1 vs 2, snel 1 vs 2, mevrouw 2 vs 1, jullie 2 vs 1, heel twice, wc twice, geen twice, three separable-verb and three perfect-tense paradigms), the roman field strips diacritics on a Latin-script language so hé and hè collapse to the same string and één becomes een, and two pronunciation respellings are simply wrong (wc "wee-say" at hs-0169 contradicting the correct "wee-see" at hs-0564; cv "say-vay" for see-vay at hs-1118). On the specific hunts: the register slips are Tast toe and zeer doen (Flemish/child), the N/A over-claims are airco (a perfectly ordinary Dutch word, wrongly blanked at hs-0460), bidden/het gebed (hs-0694), and the shoes-off claim at hs-0761 which flatly contradicts hs-1148; the two glosses I would not ship are "I'm full, honestly" (hs-0311, hospitality tic from the source) and "my stomach's upset" for buikpijn (hs-0451). Fix the duplicates and the leaked scaffold mechanically, add the ten grammar paradigms and the twenty work-and-transaction items above, and this becomes a defensible A1–A2 Dutch spine rather than a well-localised Hindi one.

The national street party, everyone in orange. Sinterklaas (5 December) is the big family one
You're legally required to carry ID from 14 – paspoort, ID-kaart or driving licence
English verbs take Dutch endings and behave like any other: checken, appen, mailen, downloaden, gamen – gechecked, gemaild, geappt.

items.word: Zet me even op de speaker
items.roman: Zet me even op de speaker

items.note: '25-jarig jubileum' – marked properly at Dutch workplaces. A wedding anniversary is 'onze trouwdag'
Singular in Dutch: 'Waar is m'n bril?'. de zonnebril = sunglasses
Missing from the list entirely, yet it is the commonest subject after ik and je. After a verb it weakens to -ie: 'komt-ie', 'heeft-ie'.

items.word: ik – je/jij – hij – ze/zij – het – we/wij – jullie – ze/zij
items.roman: ik - je/jij - hij - ze/zij - het - we/wij - jullie - ze/zij
items.note: Nearly every pronoun has a weak and a strong form; speech uses the weak one unless you are contrasting: 'Zij wel, ik niet'.

items.word: ik heb / jij hebt / hij heeft / wij hebben
items.roman: ik heb / jij hebt / hij heeft / wij hebben
items.note: The second most-used verb in Dutch and the only one missing a table here. Inversion drops the -t: heb je tijd? u heeft and u hebt are both fine.

items.word: Morgen ga ik / Om zes uur eet ik
items.roman: Morgen ga ik / Om zes uur eet ik
items.en: inversion: put anything but the subject first and the subject moves behind the verb
items.note: The verb clings to second place. 'Ik ga morgen' and 'Morgen ga ik' are both right; 'Morgen ik ga' is the single most audible British mistake.

items.word: Kom je? / Heb je tijd? / Werk jij hier?
items.roman: Kom je? / Heb je tijd? / Werk jij hier?
items.note: No do-support at all, and jij/je loses the -t: je werkt → werk je? Same drop with heb je, ben je, kun je.

items.word: wonen → ik woon; pakken → ik pak; lezen → ik lees; reizen → ik reis; schrijven → ik schrijf
items.roman: wonen -> ik woon; pakken -> ik pak; lezen -> ik lees; reizen -> ik reis
items.en: building the ik-form: drop -en, then fix the spelling
items.note: Long vowels double in a closed syllable, double consonants drop, and v/z turn into f/s at the end. Without this rule the tier-1 present tense cannot actually be produced.

items.word: Ik ken hem niet / Ik ga vandaag niet naar kantoor / Het is niet duur
items.roman: Ik ken hem niet / Ik ga vandaag niet naar kantoor / Het is niet duur
items.note: After the object and the time expression, but before an adjective, a prepositional phrase or a separable particle: 'Doe de deur niet dicht'.

items.word: Ik probeer te bellen / Ik heb geen tijd om te koken
items.roman: Ik probeer te bellen / Ik heb geen tijd om te koken
items.en: te + infinitive; om ... te for 'in order to'
items.note: Modals never take te (ik moet bellen), most other verbs do (ik probeer te bellen, ik vergeet te betalen). Nothing in the list teaches this.

items.en: the diminutive: biertje, kaartje, momentje, mannetje, boompje, koninkje
items.note: All diminutives are het-words. Half the time it has nothing to do with size – een biertje is a normal beer – it just makes the thing friendly and the request softer.

items.word: ik voel me / jij voelt je / hij voelt zich / u voelt zich
items.roman: ik voel me / jij voelt je / hij voelt zich / u voelt zich
items.note: zich only for hij/zij/het/ze and u. The everyday ones: zich voelen, zich vergissen, zich haasten, zich ziek melden, zich vervelen.

items.word: even, maar, eens, nou, wel, toch, hoor, gewoon
items.roman: even, maar, eens, nou, wel, toch, hoor, gewoon
items.en: the modal particles: the little words that make Dutch sound Dutch
items.note: 'Doe de deur even dicht' is a request; without even it is an order. Leave them all out and correct Dutch still sounds rude.
The counterweight to niet: 'Jij komt niet? Ik wel.' Also the standard hedge: 'Dat is wel lekker', 'Ik ga wel'. It appears in six notes in this list but has no item of its own.
'Ik ga gewoon', 'gewoon lekker', 'Doe maar gewoon'. One of the most frequent words in spoken Dutch.
Same meaning as omdat but keeps normal word order: 'Ik kom niet, want ik moet werken'. In speech it is far commoner than omdat, and it is the safe one while verb-final is still shaky.

items.word: Zou je ... kunnen? / Ik zou graag ...
items.roman: Zou je ... kunnen? / Ik zou graag ...
items.note: Turns a demand into a request: 'Kun je even helpen?' → 'Zou je me even kunnen helpen?' Also 'Ik zou het niet doen'.

items.word: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht
items.roman: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht
items.en: order of the extras: when – how – where
items.note: English puts place first ('to Utrecht by train tomorrow'); Dutch reverses it. Get it wrong and the sentence is understandable but audibly foreign.

items.word: g/ch, ui, ij/ei, eu, oe, and the -d that says t
items.en: the five sounds that give a British accent away
items.note: goed and acht scrape at the back; huis and uit have no English vowel; wij/mij, leuk, boek. A final -d is said as t: goed = 'goet', hond = 'hont'. Nothing else in the list touches pronunciation.
The opinion verb, and it only appears inside a chunk here: 'Wat vind je ervan?', 'Ik vind het leuk'. Also literal: 'Ik kan m'n sleutels niet vinden'.
Only mentioned in a note under kijken. kijken is looking on purpose, zien is what you see. 'Ik zie je morgen', 'Zie je dat?', 'Ik heb het gezien'.
Lives only inside chunks here, but it is a full modal: 'Mag dat?', 'Dat mag niet', 'Je mag het houden'. Also liking: 'Ik mag hem wel'.
Absent from a work-and-travel list. 'Kan ik hier pinnen?' for card, 'Mag ik afrekenen?' at a café table, 'apart betalen' to split.
Only in a note under wonen. 'Blijf je eten?', 'Het blijft droog' – the best forecast you will get.

items.en: to stand; to be (upright); to say (on a sign or screen)
items.note: 'Er staat iemand voor de deur', 'Wat staat er?' = what does it say, 'Dat staat je goed' = that suits you. Pairs with zitten and liggen, which are already in the list.

items.en: to catch, to make out (what someone said)
items.note: 'Ik versta je niet' = I can't hear you properly; 'Ik snap je niet' = I don't follow you. Two completely different complaints, and the learner needs the first one daily.
Separable: 'Zullen we iets afspreken?', 'We spreken om zes uur af'. The noun is de afspraak. Dutch social life is booked in advance, not dropped in on.
Named in five notes but never taught. You register with one in your own postcode, ring for an afspraak, and get nothing else in Dutch healthcare without a verwijzing from them.
Missing entirely. Given as street + huisnummer, or just postcode + huisnummer, which is what forms, deliveries and taxis actually ask for.
vergaderen = to meet; 'Ik zit in een vergadering'. het overleg is the smaller, informal sort: 'even overleggen'.
'Ik zet het in m'n agenda', 'Past het in je agenda?' Dutch working life runs on it – almost nothing happens unplanned.
'Ik mail je even'. Like appen: an English verb with Dutch endings – gemaild, een mailtje.
Separable: 'ik werk morgen thuis'. Standard in the Netherlands, usually on fixed days, and the first thing colleagues will ask you about.
'vakantie opnemen' = to book leave, 'vrij nemen' for a single day, 'vrije dagen' = your allowance.
The vrijdagmiddagborrel is a workplace fixture, not an optional social. borrelen is the verb, borrelhapjes the nibbles.
Buried inside one chunk here, but it is the word Dutch people will insist is untranslatable and will use about any pleasant room, evening or gathering: 'Wat gezellig!', 'Het was heel gezellig'.
The list teaches four ways to say thank you and no way to answer it. 'Geen dank' and 'geen probleem' do the same job.

items.word: Ik wil graag een afspraak maken
items.roman: Ik wil graag een afspraak maken
items.en: I'd like to make an appointment
items.note: Opens the huisarts, the tandarts, the kapper, the garage and the gemeente. Follow-up: 'Kan het deze week nog?'
On a full train, tram or shop aisle – the single most-used courtesy of a Dutch commute. 'Pardon' on its own also works.
You catch the waiter's eye and say it – nobody brings the bill unasked. 'De rekening, graag' is the same move.
The standard shop and café send-off, and you say it straight back. 'Fijn weekend' from Friday lunchtime on.
'Is er wifi?', 'Is er nog koffie?', 'Er is geen plek meer'. This existential er is the one use of er a beginner needs at once.
'Wilt u de bon?' at every till, and you need it to return anything. In speech: het bonnetje.
Four digits and two letters (1017 CD). Postcode plus huisnummer identifies any Dutch address on its own – it is what every form and delivery asks for first.
Useless on a bike, which is why people wear a regenjas or a regenpak and just get on with it.
Named in a note under kaartje but never taught. You can also tap in with your own bank card (OVpay); either way you in- and uitcheck on every leg.
You ring your manager, not HR, before the working day starts, and no doctor's note is needed. Reflexive: zich ziek melden.
You report it online at politie.nl and you will need the framenummer. Two locks is normal, and so is this sentence.
112 for police, fire and ambulance. 0900-8844 for the police when it isn't urgent, and de huisartsenpost for medical problems out of hours.
'Kunt u dat spellen?' with u. As a Brit you will be spelling your own name several times a week.
The answer to 'Kan ik u helpen?' in a shop. The list teaches how to ask for help but not how to decline it.
At the cheese counter, the pharmacy and the gemeente: 'Heeft u een nummertje?' Without one you are not in the queue.

items.en: shall I take my shoes off?
items.note: Practice genuinely varies by household, so ask rather than guess – which is also the fix for the flat 'shoes stay on' claim at hs-0761.
Needed for tax, health insurance, the gemeente and your GP portal. You get one after you inschrijven at the gemeente and receive your BSN (burgerservicenummer).
Compulsory once you work here, and backdated if you're late. het eigen risico is the excess you pay before it starts covering anything.
The list teaches the question ('Wat voor werk doe je?') but not the answer: 'Ik werk bij een bank als analist.'
